questions.q: Why does SSH show a host key fingerprint and ask for confirmation the first time you connect to a new server?
options: It's generating a new password for that session
It's recording the server's identity so it can warn you later if that identity changes unexpectedly
It's a required step to enable encryption at all
It's checking whether the server has enough disk space
questions.explain: SSH records the server's host key fingerprint on first connection. If a future connection presents a different fingerprint for the same host, SSH warns you — which could indicate a rebuilt server or a potential attack.

questions.q: In SSH public-key authentication, which key stays on your own machine and is never shared?
options: The public key
The private key
Both keys are shared with the server
Neither key — only a password is used
questions.explain: The private key never leaves your machine. The public key is the half you distribute to servers you want to access; the server uses it to verify a challenge only the matching private key could answer.

options: Generates a brand new SSH key pair on the remote server
Appends your local public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the remote server
Changes the remote user's password
Deletes any existing keys on the remote server
questions.explain: ssh-copy-id copies your public key (not private) to the remote account's authorized_keys file, enabling future passwordless logins for that key.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a passphrase set on a private key during `ssh-keygen`?
options: It replaces the need for a public key entirely
It encrypts the private key file itself, adding protection if the key file is ever stolen
It is sent to the server as an additional password
It has no real security purpose
questions.explain: A passphrase encrypts the private key on disk. Even if someone copies the private key file, they still need the passphrase to use it — it never gets transmitted over the network.

questions.q: What does a `Host` entry in `~/.ssh/config` let you do?
options: Block a specific host from ever being reached
Define a short alias for a host along with its hostname, username, and key, so `ssh <alias>` connects without typing the full details
Automatically generate a new key pair for that host
Store your password for that host in plain text
questions.explain: ~/.ssh/config lets you map a short alias (Host) to connection details like HostName, User, and IdentityFile, so both ssh and scp can use the shorthand instead of the full command every time.
